prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency.

statement.case_for: I opened with the Higgs observation (B055) because I think the prize should go to discoveries first and people second, and I still regard that discovery as the clearest in the list. But after reading the other seven ballots I have to weigh it differently: it is the only shortlisted entry on which I stand alone, and my own opening admitted that no fair three-person split exists among five credited names. Setting that aside, the strongest remaining case is B005. Optical lattice clocks are a clean invention with a decisive conceptual step (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping) and a decisive demonstration of ultimate performance (Ye's clocks at the 1e-18 level). Seven of eight members ranked it, five put it in their top three, every one of them proposed exactly the same two names, and the attribution is the least contested on the shortlist. The work has been reproduced and surpassed in many independent laboratories over two decades, it constrains tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy, and the pending redefinition of the second gives it a concrete future. Of the shortlisted entries it combines the highest maturity with the cleanest credit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is a measurement-science and instrumentation achievement, closely adjacent to the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, so a committee that wants conceptual novelty rather than ever-better precision could judge it incremental. Some of its payoff is prospective until the SI second is actually redefined. A second reservation is that the Katori-Ye pairing leaves out other lattice-clock groups and ultrastable-laser contributors, and I cannot verify from the supplied material that they are less decisive. If the committee prefers a case where nature surprised us (my own instinct, as in my attributed remark that physicists must find clues in nature), B014 deserves to outrank it.

responses.point: Kroll ranks lattice clocks first on the argument that progress is bounded by how accurately we can measure, and asks whether the committee would prefer to group clocks with ultrastable-laser or comb work.
responses.response: I agree with the measurement argument, and it is the reason I move B005 above my own opening rank of five. I disagree with grouping it with ultrastable-laser or comb work: that would blur a clean two-person credit into a diffuse technology prize, and the comb was already recognised in 2005. The magic-wavelength idea plus its record-accuracy realization is a self-contained discovery-grade invention and should be cited as such.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and led the first realization while Ye brought it to record accuracy, and that the contribution is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes.
responses.response: That is the point that persuades me most on overlap. From outside atomic physics I worried about a third precision-measurement prize in two decades, and your distinction between ion clocks, combs and many-atom lattice interrogation answers it. I would still ask you to be precise about Ye's share: is it a co-invention or primarily a demonstration of ultimate performance? The citation I propose treats it as invention and realization jointly, but I would want the committee to test that wording.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, calling it a clean theory-plus-experiment prize that is timely rather than premature, with the superconducting mechanism unsettled but the discovery stable.
responses.response: I take this seriously, and it is why B014 is my first alternative and why I ranked it fourth. Where I qualify your view is on maturity and attribution: the 2018 experiments are only eight years old, the pairing mechanism and several correlated phases are still contested, and Cao as first author, Dean and others, and earlier twisted-bilayer theorists (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) complicate a three-person list in a way they do not for Katori and Ye. If this committee cares about robustness of credit, B005 is safer; if it values a surprising new platform, your case is stronger than mine and I would not resist it.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos first, arguing that the deep-ice detection concept was unproven, delivered a stable diffuse flux, and that Halzen and Spiering are central, while noting the DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA pioneers.
responses.response: I ranked B035 sixth, so I do not dismiss it; it is a genuine discovery of a new window, which is the kind of case I care about. My difficulty is the one you name yourself: a large single collaboration, a pioneer chain from DUMAND and Baikal to AMANDA, and only partial source identification. You propose two names where Mehlig and I propose two or three different combinations, which shows how arbitrary the cut is. I would rather see the committee settle B005 first and revisit IceCube once the source picture matures.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, while openly flagging a possible bias from working in the area and noting that Wallraff, who did the first strong-coupling experiment, is not among the credited names.
responses.response: I respect that you flagged your own bias. The omission of Wallraff is exactly the kind of attribution gap that makes B046 harder for me than the clock case. Proximity to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits, which Kroll and Lindroth both raise, also weighs against it for this year. I do not think the scientific merit is in doubt, but I would not put it ahead of a candidate with an unambiguous credit list.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the KPZ universality class first, calling it a central organizing concept of non-equilibrium statistical physics, while acknowledging that Parisi, an original author, is outside the credited names.
responses.response: The KPZ equation is a profoundly important idea, and I share your view that it is mature. But you identify the central problem yourself: the 1986 paper has three authors and the supplied list omits one of them in favour of Spohn's later rigorous programme, so any prize built on these names would look incomplete or would credit a different achievement than the original equation. I cannot support it as the preferred configuration unless the committee is willing to cite the exact-solution programme instead of the equation, and that is a different prize with different laureates.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards another precision-measurement prize so soon after the 2005 and 2012 prizes as an acceptable use of a slot, or would prefer a more conceptually surprising case.
Whether Ye's contribution is best described as co-invention or as record-accuracy realization, which affects how the citation should be worded.
Whether B014 should outrank B005 once the debate over the superconducting mechanism and the Cao, Dean and early-theory credit questions is weighed; I am close to indifferent between them.

The Higgs discovery (B055) still seems to me scientifically compelling, but I do not see a defensible three-person allocation among Gianotti, Evans, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, and no colleague has supported it, so I treat it as an alternative only.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred B005 (Katori, Ye) or for B014. My documented connections are my PhD supervisor David Gross, early mentor Hector Rubinstein, co-author Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, none of whom are among the credited names. My two years at CERN after the PhD is a general institutional link to the Higgs-related entry B055 (an alternative), but my profile records no tie to any of its named individuals.
